title: the bridge
hook: the war book opens with an embrace, a march, and a sea nobody can cross

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line, tell me her words again: a jewel from her hair, a crow story only Rama would know, one month on the clock. That closed the Sundara Kanda. Today the sixth book, the Yuddha Kanda, the war book, begins. Day six hundred thirty-four.

The war book doesn't open with a war. It opens with a thank-you. Rama turns to Hanuman and tries to say what he's done: crossed an ocean, found her, come back. Then Rama looks at himself. He's an exile in bark clothes, living on a mountain. He has no kingdom to share, no treasury, no land to give. So he says the one gift he has left is this, and he takes Hanuman in his arms. The epic's sixth book begins with an embrace, from a man who has nothing else to offer.
screen: `NOT A WAR. A THANK-YOU.` → `NOTHING LEFT TO GIVE.` → `AN EMBRACE.`

segments.voice: Then the thank-you turns into a question. Hanuman crossed the ocean alone, by leaping. An army can't leap. Rama says it plainly: how will all of us get across? Sugriva answers like a good friend in a crisis. Grief makes a person slow, he says. Let's move, and find the way when we're there. So the army marches south. Valmiki makes it huge and noisy: the monkey and bear troops spreading over hills and forests, Sugriva and Lakshmana beside Rama, Hanuman carrying him on his shoulders at times. They reach the southern shore and make camp at the edge of the land. And there it is. The ocean, as Valmiki paints it, roaring, full of sea creatures, rising and falling as if it were breathing, with no other shore in sight. That night, Rama can't rest. He stands at the edge of the water and speaks to the wind. You blow where she is, he says. Touch her, and then come and touch me. The general who has to cross the sea is also a husband standing on a beach in the dark. Hold onto this picture: the army behind him, the water in front, and no way over. Everything in the next few days is the answer to it. A bridge doesn't begin with stones. It begins with someone standing at the edge, admitting there's no way across yet.
screen: `HOW WILL WE ALL GET ACROSS?` · `THE ARMY MARCHES SOUTH.` · `THE OCEAN WITH NO FAR SHORE.` · `RAMA SPEAKS TO THE WIND.` · then, large: `A BRIDGE BEGINS AT THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Picture something in your life right now that feels like that ocean: a gap you can't see across yet. Don't try to solve it. Just stand at the edge of it for a moment, the way Rama stood on the shore. Name it to yourself, honestly. Breathe in. Breathe out. Standing at the edge and naming it is the first stone. The bell holds the time.
The bridge. Setu in Sanskrit. Before there's a single stone, there's an army on a beach, a sea with no far shore, and a question: how do we all get across?
Your line: an army on a beach. Today, name one gap you can't see across yet, and let naming it be enough for now. Day six hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: The Yuddha Kanda is the longest book of Valmiki's Ramayana; Hindu storytellers and reciters often open it with Rama's embrace of Hanuman, a moment many devotees of Hanuman treasure.

original.note: Sanskrit setu: a bridge or causeway, also a dike or boundary.

notes: Rama's words that the embrace is all he can give (Yuddha 1, sarvasva-bhūtaḥ pariṣvaṅgaḥ): paraphrased; confirm.
Hanuman carrying Rama and Angada carrying Lakshmana on the march (Yuddha 4): confirm.
Rama's speech to the wind (Yuddha 5): paraphrased loosely; confirm the sense.
The Yuddha Kanda as the longest book: confirm for the critical and vulgate editions.
In Valmiki, Vibhishana's crossing comes before the bridge; the outline places the bridge first (days 634–636) and Vibhishana after (637–638). Day 637 tells it as a step back in time.
